stimulus.text: Paraphrase: More than a million Black Americans served in the armed forces during World War II, most of them in segregated units. The best-known Black combat units were the Tuskegee Airmen, the first Black military pilots, who flew escort missions over Europe, and the 761st Tank Battalion. Japanese American soldiers of the 442nd Regimental Combat Team fought in Italy and France while many of their families were held in relocation camps at home. Navajo Marines in the Pacific sent radio messages in a code built on the Navajo language that Japanese code-breakers never broke. Black leaders called the fight the 'Double V': victory over fascism abroad and victory over racism at home.
stimulus.source_note: Original secondary summary drawn from Barron's Chapter 9 (Tuskegee Airmen; 761st Tank Battalion; Double V; 1.2 million Black Americans served; desegregation in 1948) and standard accounts of the 442nd Regimental Combat Team and the Navajo code talkers, verified against public sources. The books do not name the 442nd or the code talkers; both are named in the topic scope.

source: original; stimulus drawn from book-grounded figures and paraphrases (see source_note)
stem: The passage describes the 442nd Regimental Combat Team fighting in Europe while their families were held in camps. What does that contrast best illustrate about the war?

options.text: Japanese American soldiers were not allowed to fight at all
options.misconception: The 442nd fought in Italy and France; Japanese Americans did serve.

options.text: The camps were built to train soldiers for combat
options.misconception: The camps held families, including children, not soldiers in training.

options.text: Soldiers from a group the government distrusted still served with distinction
The government released all internees as soon as the 442nd was formed
options.misconception: Most internees stayed in the camps until the war was nearly over.

rationales.A: The 442nd fought in Italy and France, so Japanese Americans did serve.
rationales.B: The camps held civilian families, not soldiers in training.
rationales.C: The 442nd served with distinction while their families were held in camps.
rationales.D: Most internees stayed in the camps until late in the war.
rationales.general:
1. The passage says the 442nd fought in Italy and France.
2. It also says many of their families were held in relocation camps at home.
3. Background: the government had removed Japanese Americans from the West Coast as suspected enemies.
4. Yet the soldiers of the 442nd became one of the most decorated units of the war.
Remember: a contrast between treatment and service shows what service had to overcome.
